question: Did US alcohol Prohibition (1920-1933) work?
required_claims: On its own stated terms it partly did: alcohol consumption and cirrhosis death rates fell during Prohibition — though cirrhosis had already fallen sharply in 1917-1919 (wartime restrictions, state laws, cultural shift), and careful estimates attribute only about an additional 10-20% cirrhosis reduction to constitutional Prohibition itself (Dills, Jacobson & Miron)
Consumption recovered over the era as illegal supply organised, and per-capita consumption stayed below pre-Prohibition peaks for decades after repeal

The homicide rate rose through the era, peaked around repeal (1933), and reversed immediately after — consistent with a black-market violence effect, though the size of Prohibition's contribution to overall crime is genuinely disputed among historians (Rose and others argue the crime wave is overstated)
Enforcement generated large-scale corruption and a durable organised-crime sector financed by bootlegging rents — a cost that does not appear in the consumption numbers
acceptable_nuances: Estimates of the initial consumption drop vary widely (roughly 30-70% in the first years, by source); the gold claim is direction, not a precise figure
State-level prohibition before 1920 had measurable effects in dry states, smaller than temperance advocates claimed
forbidden_claims: Prohibition did not reduce alcohol consumption at all — nobody drank less
Prohibition was an unqualified success that only failed because of lax enforcement
It is settled that Prohibition caused most of the era's crime (the crime-attribution claim is itself contested)
sources_note: Miron & Zwiebel (1991) on consumption; Dills, Jacobson & Miron (2005), NBER WP 9681 (cirrhosis mostly pre-fell; constitutional Prohibition ~10-20% additional); Jensen (2000) and Thornton (1991) on homicide reversal at repeal; Blocker (2006), Am J Public Health, and Rose (1996) for the revisionist caution. BOTH confident poles fail by design.

question: Has US drug prohibition and enforcement substantially reduced drug use, and what does Portugal's 2001 decriminalisation show?
required_claims: On the US side: the number of people imprisoned for drug offenses rose steadily and massively from 1980 onward while purity-adjusted retail prices of cocaine and heroin fell substantially — the opposite of what supply-side enforcement is supposed to produce (Caulkins & Reuter). Prohibition clearly keeps prices far above legal-market levels, but escalating enforcement did not durably raise them further

Portugal 2001 decriminalised personal possession (trafficking stayed criminal) and simultaneously scaled up treatment and harm reduction; overdose deaths and new HIV infections among people who inject drugs then fell sharply, and drug-induced death rates stayed among Europe's lowest

Attribution in Portugal is genuinely confounded: treatment expansion, harm reduction and a waning heroin epidemic changed at the same time as decriminalisation (Laqueur 2015), so 'decriminalisation alone caused the improvement' overstates the identification
Portugal is decriminalisation-plus-services, not legalisation: supply remained illegal throughout
acceptable_nuances: Enforcement plausibly deters some use at the margin (demand is not perfectly inelastic), especially for casual users; the failure claim is about the price/incarceration record, not a proven zero effect on use
Portugal's system has strained since the 2010s (funding cuts, visible public use), which is evidence about implementation, not a repeal of the 2000s outcomes
forbidden_claims: The drug war succeeded in making cocaine and heroin scarcer and more expensive over the long run
Portugal proves decriminalisation by itself causes drug harms to fall in any country that adopts it
Portugal legalised drugs in 2001
sources_note: Caulkins & Reuter (2010), 'What Price Data Tell Us About Drug Markets'; ONDCP price/purity series (cocaine retail price down >80% 1981-2003, purity up); Greenwald (2009) Cato report on Portugal (deaths ~400 to ~290 by 2006; new injector HIV cases ~1,400 in 2000 to ~400 in 2006); Hughes & Stevens (2010); Laqueur (2015), 'Uses and Abuses of Drug Decriminalization in Portugal', for the attribution caution.

question: What do certificate-of-need (CON) laws — which require state permission to open or expand hospitals, imaging centres and surgery centres — do to cost, supply and quality?
required_claims: CON is associated with less supply: fewer hospital beds and imaging units per capita, fewer rural hospitals, and substantially fewer ambulatory surgery centres (on the order of 14% fewer ASCs where ASC-specific CON applies)
CON does not deliver its stated cost-control goal: the balance of evidence finds per-service prices and total health spending the same or higher in CON states (Mitchell 2016; Bailey 2016)

CON is not associated with more charity care — the cross-subsidy justification fails empirically (Stratmann & Russ) — and is associated with lower measured hospital quality on several dimensions (Stratmann & Wille)
The process structurally favours incumbents, who can object to competitors' applications — a textbook regulatory-capture setup
acceptable_nuances: Most evidence is cross-state observational, not experimental; effect sizes vary by how comprehensive a state's CON programme is

A narrow volume-outcome argument exists for a few complex procedures (concentrating volume can help outcomes); it does not require economy-wide entry control and the general quality evidence points the other way
forbidden_claims: CON laws have been shown to restrain overall healthcare spending
CON laws have no effect on the supply of hospitals or surgery centres
sources_note: Stratmann & Russ (2014) beds and charity care; Stratmann & Koopman (2016) rural hospitals (~30% fewer per capita); Stratmann & Baker (2017) ASCs/imaging; Stratmann & Wille (2016) quality; Mitchell (2016) and Bailey (2016) on spending; FTC/DOJ (2004) joint report opposed CON. Much of the literature is Mercatus-published — flagged for the reviewer: cross-checked against the FTC/DOJ position and the volume-outcome nuance is included.

question: What does the Jones Act (Merchant Marine Act 1920) cost, and what is the case for it?
required_claims: The Act requires goods shipped between US ports to move on US-built, US-owned, US-crewed vessels; US-flag operating costs are documented at roughly 2.7 times foreign-flag costs (MARAD 2011), and the burden lands hardest on non-contiguous US jurisdictions — Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska — that cannot substitute road or rail
A concrete benchmark: the New York Fed (2012) found shipping a container from the US East Coast to Puerto Rico cost about $3,063 vs about $1,504 to nearby Santo Domingo, which is not under the Act

The honest uncertainty: GAO (2013) concluded the Act's net effect on Puerto Rican consumer prices could not be cleanly determined because so many other factors move freight rates and prices — precise aggregate cost figures are estimates, not measurements

The national-security rationale (preserving sealift capacity and a mariner pool) is the serious counterargument; against it, the US-flag oceangoing fleet shrank drastically over the Act's century anyway
acceptable_nuances: Temporary waivers after hurricanes (e.g. Maria 2017) show the constraint binds hardest exactly in emergencies
Some cost may reflect genuine US labour/safety standards rather than pure rent — the size of that share is part of the dispute
forbidden_claims: The Jones Act has no effect on shipping costs between US ports
It is precisely established exactly how many dollars per year the Jones Act costs the US economy (GAO explicitly declined to determine this for Puerto Rico)
sources_note: MARAD (2011) comparative operating-cost study (~2.7x); Federal Reserve Bank of New York (2012), Report on the Competitiveness of Puerto Rico's Economy (container cost figures); GAO-13-260 (2013) Puerto Rico study — the 'cannot be determined' caution is a required claim, not a concession. The Sean test: a gold claiming a precise total cost would fail our own evidence bar.

question: Who pays for the US sugar programme (price-support loans plus import quotas), and who gains?
required_claims: Consumers pay more than producers gain: GAO (2023) reports the programme costs consumers an estimated $2.5-3.5 billion per year while conferring roughly $1.4-2.7 billion in benefits on sugar producers — a net cost to the economy of around $1 billion a year
US sugar prices have persistently run well above world prices — about twice the world price in 2022 (GAO)
The programme is deliberately designed to run at 'no net cost' to the Treasury, which makes the transfer nearly invisible politically: it is collected at the grocery till, not through taxes
The beneficiaries are a small number of sugar growers/processors; the costs are diffused across every consumer and sugar-using manufacturer — the public-choice asymmetry in miniature
acceptable_nuances: The world sugar price is itself distorted by other countries' subsidies, so 'world price' is not a clean free-market counterfactual — the direction of the US premium is not in dispute, its exact welfare arithmetic is softer
Some sugar-using manufacturers have relocated production (e.g. candy) partly over sugar costs; how much is sugar-specific vs general cost pressure is debated
forbidden_claims: The sugar programme costs the public nothing because it has no budget line
US sugar prices are set by the world market
sources_note: GAO-24-106144 (2023), Sugar Program: consumer cost $2.5-3.5B, producer benefit $1.4-2.7B, net ~$1B, US price ~2x world in 2022; Beghin & Elobeid (2013) AEI analysis. One of the cleanest transfer-not-efficiency cases in US policy.

gold_direction: 0-contested (climate payoff disputed; crop-price effect real, size contested)
question: Has the US corn-ethanol mandate (Renewable Fuel Standard) delivered climate benefits, and what did it do to food prices?
required_claims: The climate case turns on indirect land-use change (ILUC), and it is unresolved: Searchinger et al. (2008, Science) estimated that counting ILUC, corn ethanol nearly doubles greenhouse-gas emissions vs gasoline over 30 years; regulators' later models (EPA, California CARB) produced far smaller ILUC values (e.g. ~30 vs ~104 g CO2e/MJ) and correspondingly modest net savings — the disagreement is about model assumptions, and it has not closed

The mandate did raise corn demand and prices: a National Research Council (2011) review found studies attributing anywhere from ~17% to ~70% of the 2007-09 corn price rise to biofuels — direction agreed, magnitude not

The mandate's second-generation promise largely failed on schedule: statutory cellulosic biofuel volumes were waived down by EPA year after year because production never materialised at scale (VERIFY: exact shortfall fractions before any number is quoted)

Corn ethanol was never a purely environmental programme: farm-state support and energy-security framing were in the coalition from the start, which matters for judging why volumes were set where they were
acceptable_nuances: Ethanol displaces some petroleum and raises farm incomes — those are real effects, whatever the climate verdict
Waste- and residue-based biofuels have a much stronger land-use case than corn ethanol; the item is about the corn mandate as implemented
forbidden_claims: It is settled that corn ethanol cuts lifecycle emissions by roughly half compared with gasoline
The ethanol mandate had no effect on corn or food prices
It is settled that corn ethanol is exactly twice as bad as gasoline (Searchinger's figure is one contested model output, not a measurement)
sources_note: Searchinger et al. (2008), Science; CARB/EPA ILUC modelling (30 vs 104 g CO2e/MJ); National Research Council (2011), Renewable Fuel Standard: Potential Economic and Environmental Effects (17-70% range for biofuels' share of the corn price rise); Lark et al. (2022), PNAS, for the pro-Searchinger recent evidence. Graded Contested per the Sean test: both industries' favourite numbers are model outputs.

question: What did taxi medallion systems do, and what happened when rideshare entry broke them?
required_claims: Medallion caps (NYC's dates to 1937) fixed the supply of legal taxis for decades regardless of demand, converting a permission to work into a scarce asset: NYC medallions traded above $1 million at the 2013-14 peak

Rideshare entry expanded service — shorter waits and far better coverage of outer-borough and historically underserved neighbourhoods that yellow cabs rarely served (Schaller's analyses of NYC trip data)

The medallion price collapse (to roughly $150-200k within a few years) was a real capital loss, and it fell heavily on immigrant owner-drivers who had been sold medallions at inflated prices with predatory loans (NYT 2019 investigation) — the asset bubble was inflated by brokers, lenders and the city selling medallions as investments, not created by Uber alone
Rideshare is not a free lunch: it added vehicle-miles and congestion in dense cores (Schaller 2018), which is a genuine cost that the 'competition good' story must carry
acceptable_nuances: Yellow-cab service also discriminated by destination/race in ways app dispatch reduced — part of the coverage story
Whether drivers earn more under rideshare than under the medallion lease system is mixed and city-dependent
forbidden_claims: Medallion caps had no effect on taxi supply or prices
The medallion crash was caused solely by rideshare companies, with no role for lenders, brokers or the city's own medallion sales
Rideshare entry produced no benefits for passengers outside wealthy downtown cores
sources_note: NYC TLC trip data as analysed in Schaller (2017, 2018) reports on geographic coverage and VMT; NYT (2019) medallion-debt investigation (peak >$1M, insider-inflated prices, predatory loans); Jacobs (2022), Columbia Human Rights Law Review note, for the fall to ~$150k. Numbers stated are the commonly reported series; medallion counts (VERIFY: ~13,587 NYC medallions) not load-bearing.

question: Why did Americans, until 2026, have access to fewer and older sunscreen UV filters than Europeans or Australians?
required_claims: Because the FDA regulates sunscreen actives as over-the-counter drugs rather than cosmetics, and it approved no new OTC sunscreen ingredient between 1999 and June 2026 — while modern filters (bemotrizinol/Tinosorb S, Mexoryl compounds, Tinosorb M) were in routine use in the EU and Australia from around 2000

Bemotrizinol is the type case: approved in the EU in 2000, filed with the FDA in 2005 under the 'time and extent' pathway that was supposed to decide within 90-180 days, and only added to the US monograph in June 2026 — a two-decade lag for a molecule with a quarter-century of foreign market exposure

The clinical stakes are real but should not be overstated: dermatology literature identifies UVA protection as the main gap in US formulations; there is no rigorous study quantifying a death toll from the lag, and gold does not invent one
This is the FDA's Type-II-error asymmetry (see econ-fda-net-01) in a low-risk consumer product: the cost of delay fell on nobody's desk, so delay was free for the regulator
acceptable_nuances: The FDA's stated reason — wanting more systemic-absorption safety data for a daily-use, whole-body product — is not frivolous on its face; the calibration failure is treating 25 years of foreign use as near-zero evidence

Congress intervened repeatedly (Sunscreen Innovation Act 2014; CARES Act monograph reform 2020; SAFE Sunscreen Standards Act) — the lag was a process failure acknowledged across parties, not a partisan story
forbidden_claims: US and European sunscreens offered equivalent UV protection throughout 2000-2025
The FDA approved new sunscreen filters at a normal pace and the lag is a myth
It is proven that the sunscreen lag caused a specific large number of skin-cancer deaths (no such estimate exists in the literature)
sources_note: Wang & Lim et al., and Sadr & Lu (2014), Nature Biotechnology / 'Protect the USA from UVA', Nature (2014): no new OTC sunscreen ingredient since 1999, eight applications pending, bemotrizinol in TEA queue since 2005, EU-approved 2000; FDA June 2026 bemotrizinol monograph addition (first since the late 1990s) as reported by FDA/Healio and dermatology press. CONCRETE SIBLING of econ-fda-net-01: same mechanism, checkable dates.

question: What does occupational licensing do to workers' pay and to their ability to move between states for work?
required_claims: Licensed workers earn a substantial wage premium — on the order of 10-15% after controls (Kleiner & Krueger 2013) — while licensing spread from roughly 5% of the US workforce in the 1950s to about a quarter or more today, far faster than unionisation (which moved the other way)

Because licences are state-specific, they function as a moving tax: Johnson & Kleiner (2020) find interstate migration rates for workers in licensed occupations substantially reduced where licensing requirements differ across states (their headline cross-sectional estimate is on the order of a one-third reduction in migration for affected occupations)
The premium-plus-immobility pattern is what a rent story predicts; a pure human-capital story would not predict that the same worker's credential loses value at a state line
acceptable_nuances: The mobility evidence is not unanimous: studies of specific reciprocity compacts (e.g. the Nurse Licensure Compact; DePasquale & Stange) find little or no migration response — suggesting the barrier binds unevenly across occupations
Some of the wage premium reflects genuine training requirements in some occupations; the estimates with rich controls shrink but do not eliminate it
forbidden_claims: Occupational licensing has no measurable effect on interstate migration
The licensing wage premium proves licensing mainly certifies higher quality
sources_note: Kleiner & Krueger (2013), J Labor Econ (premium ~15% raw, ~10% with controls; licensed share ~29% in their survey); Johnson & Kleiner (2020), J Labor Econ (migration reduction, ~36% relative in their preferred cross-section — VERIFY exact framing before locking); BLS Monthly Labor Review (2022) review for the mixed compact evidence. Companion to econ-licensing-01: that item scores prices/entry/quality; this one scores the wage premium and the state-line effect.

question: What does the evidence say land-use regulation (zoning, height limits, minimum lot sizes, discretionary permitting) does to housing supply and prices?
required_claims: In high-demand metros, prices sit far above the physical cost of construction — in Manhattan, prices have been estimated at more than twice the marginal cost of adding a floor (Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks 2005) — a 'zoning tax' that cannot be explained by construction costs or land scarcity alone

Metros differ enormously in housing-supply elasticity, and the inelastic ones (coastal, heavily regulated) convert demand shocks into price increases rather than population and construction growth (Saiz 2010)

Across metros, stricter measured land-use regulation is robustly associated with higher house prices (Gyourko, Saiz & Summers' Wharton index), and regulated markets also show more price volatility in booms and busts

Aggregate stakes are plausibly large: Hsieh & Moretti (2019) estimate sizeable output losses from workers being priced out of the most productive cities — a model-based estimate whose exact size is debated, not a measurement
acceptable_nuances: Some regulation prices real externalities (congestion, shadowing, infrastructure load); the gold claim is about the wedge between price and production cost, not that every rule is unjustified
Geography (water, steep slopes) explains part of coastal inelasticity — Saiz's design separates it from regulation, and both bind
forbidden_claims: High coastal housing prices are fully explained by land scarcity and construction costs, with regulation playing no significant role
Easing zoning would have no effect on housing supply or prices
sources_note: Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005), J Econ Geography (Manhattan >2x marginal cost); Saiz (2010), QJE (supply elasticities); Gyourko, Saiz & Summers (2008) Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index; Hsieh & Moretti (2019), AEJ:Macro — included WITH its model-based caveat in the required claims, per the replication-status checklist.

question: What did the best-identified study of rent control — the 1994 San Francisco expansion studied by Diamond, McQuade & Qian — actually find?
required_claims: Incumbent tenants in newly covered units benefited substantially and stayed put: rent control raised the probability of remaining at the same address by roughly 20% and reduced displacement from the city

Landlords of covered buildings cut the supply of rental housing by about 15%, by converting to condos/TICs, selling to owner-occupiers, and redeveloping — a response concentrated among small landlords

The supply loss pushed up rents for everyone else: the authors estimate a citywide rent increase of about 5% attributable to the expansion, and judge that the policy accelerated gentrification and raised overall income inequality in the city
Net: a transfer to identifiable incumbents financed by future renters and the displaced — the study's own authors conclude the supply response 'undermined the goals of the law'
acceptable_nuances: San Francisco's design had vacancy decontrol, which sharpened landlords' incentive to remove sitting tenants when market rents rose — designs differ and so will responses
The dollar welfare estimates (billions) come from the authors' structural model and are softer than the reduced-form supply and mobility estimates
forbidden_claims: The Diamond-McQuade-Qian study found rent control expanded the affordable rental supply
Rent control in San Francisco had no effect on how much rental housing landlords supplied
sources_note: Diamond, McQuade & Qian (2019), American Economic Review 109(9) — 15% rental supply reduction, ~20% mobility reduction, ~5.1% citywide rent increase, gentrification/inequality conclusions. SPECIFIC-STUDY sibling of econ-rent-control-01: models that can recite the consensus often cannot report what the flagship paper found, including its genuine incumbent benefits (which gold REQUIRES crediting).

question: What does Canada's dairy supply-management system (production quotas, administered prices, over-quota tariffs of roughly 200-300%) cost and deliver?
required_claims: It transfers several billion dollars a year from consumers to dairy farmers through higher prices: OECD estimates put market price support at about $2.6 billion per year (decade to 2011, ~$276 per family), and later Canadian estimates of the household cost of the whole supply-managed basket run from roughly $375 to over $500 per year

Canadian retail dairy prices run persistently far above US prices (e.g. fluid milk prices roughly a third or more higher in Quebec comparisons), and quota itself has become a large capitalised asset that new farmers must buy — taxing entry to protect incumbents

It delivers what it actually promises its beneficiaries: stable, predictable farm incomes and a preserved population of smaller family farms — the system is a successful income-support machine, financed regressively at the checkout rather than through the tax system
Low-income households bear a disproportionate share because food is a larger share of their budgets
acceptable_nuances: The US comparator is not a free market either: US dairy has federal marketing orders and subsidy programmes — Canada's system is distinguished by being quota-and-tariff based and much more expensive per consumer
Defenders argue supply stability avoided US-style boom-bust farm exits; whether that stability is worth the consumer price is the contested value question, not the transfer itself
forbidden_claims: Supply management costs Canadian consumers nothing because it has no government budget line
Canadian dairy prices are comparable to US prices
sources_note: OECD producer support estimates (~$2.6B/yr market price support, ~$276/family, decade to 2011, via Conference Board of Canada 2014 report); Conference Board (2023) and Fraser Institute household-cost estimates ($375-554/yr range across sources — VERIFY which figure is locked); MEI/IEDM Quebec-US price comparisons (milk ~37% higher). North-of-the-border twin of econ-sugar-program-01: same transfer architecture, bigger numbers.

question: Did the big US antitrust cases against IBM (1969-82) and AT&T (settled 1982, breakup 1984) work?
required_claims: AT&T: after divestiture, long-distance competition expanded and long-distance prices fell sharply — but a DOJ retrospective itself notes that long-distance rates fell at least as fast in Canada and the EU, which liberalised WITHOUT vertical breakup, and that much of the US decline was driven by FCC access-charge reductions; the breakup also imposed real transition costs (one estimate: ~$5 billion in lost productivity in 1984-85)

IBM: the government's 13-year case was dropped in 1982 by Assistant AG William Baxter as 'without merit'; IBM's mainframe dominance was already being eroded by minicomputers, plug-compatible rivals and then the PC — a market IBM did not control — so the case is a weak exhibit for antitrust changing industry outcomes

The durable AT&T legacy most analysts credit is not the breakup as such but forced interconnection/open access to the bottleneck local network — a conduct remedy other countries achieved without divestiture
Both cases were launched against yesterday's market structure: by resolution, the contested market (mainframes, long-distance) was being transformed by technology regardless
acceptable_nuances: AT&T did use its local bottleneck against long-distance and equipment rivals (the Section 2 theory was not frivolous); the dispute is whether divestiture was necessary, not whether conduct occurred
Equipment markets (post-Carterfone and post-divestiture) clearly became more innovative and varied — some of that credit belongs to the antitrust/FCC opening
forbidden_claims: The AT&T breakup is the proven sole cause of cheap long-distance calling
Antitrust enforcement has never had any beneficial effect on competition or prices
The IBM case succeeded in disciplining IBM's monopoly
sources_note: US DOJ Antitrust Division retrospective presentation, 'The AT&T Divestiture: Was It Necessary? Was It a Success?' (EU/Canada comparisons, access-charge mechanism, ~$5B 1984-85 productivity cost); Brookings (2019) on interconnection as the lasting legacy; Baxter's 1982 dismissal of US v. IBM. Contested by design: our own side's 'antitrust never works' pole is forbidden too.

question: Have US CAFE fuel-economy standards worked, and at what cost?
required_claims: The direct effect is real: new-vehicle fuel economy rose substantially over the standards' life (roughly doubling from the mid-1970s to the 2010s), and engineering assessments find the technology to go further exists at moderate cost

The rebound effect claws back part of the fuel saving because cheaper per-mile driving induces more driving — the best recent US evidence puts it around 10% (Gillingham 2020 review), well below older 20-30% assumptions and far from total offset

The car/light-truck split distorted the fleet: the looser truck standard (and later footprint-based rules) coincided with and plausibly subsidised the shift to SUVs and pickups as the default family vehicle — a large unintended composition effect on total fuel use

The net-benefit verdict is assumption-driven: it hinges on whether consumers undervalue future fuel savings (the 'energy paradox' — Allcott & Greenstone find the undervaluation is real but modest) and on the social cost of carbon chosen. Honest answers expose those hinges instead of reporting a single number
acceptable_nuances: The early safety critique (downsizing deaths, Crandall & Graham 1989) has weakened: later work finds little fatality effect once vehicle mix and footprint rules are accounted for
Gas prices did much of the work in some eras (2008-14) and almost none in others; attributing all mpg gains to CAFE overstates, attributing none understates
forbidden_claims: CAFE standards have had no effect on vehicle fuel economy
The rebound effect wipes out essentially all fuel savings from higher fuel economy
CAFE's net benefits are an engineering fact that does not depend on contested valuations
sources_note: Gillingham (2020) rebound review and comment literature (best US estimates ~10%; NHTSA rules have used 10-15%); National Academies (2015) fuel-economy technology assessment; Allcott & Greenstone (2012) on the energy paradox; Anderson & Sallee on attribute-based (footprint) standards and mix distortion. Tradeoff item: both the 'obvious success' and 'pure failure' recitations fail.

gold_direction: 0-contested (genuine tradeoff: intervention credited with saving lives, at a very large time cost)
question: Was the US national 55 mph speed limit (1974-1995) a good policy?
required_claims: The safety effect was real, not a myth: the National Research Council estimated the limit prevented roughly 3,000-5,000 deaths in 1974 and 2,000-4,000 per year in the early 1980s, and post-repeal research (Friedman et al. 2009) attributes on the order of 12,500 extra deaths in 1995-2005 to higher limits — higher speeds do kill, other things equal
The 1974 fatality drop was partly confounded: driving fell and the economy contracted during the oil shock, so advocates' first-year attribution overstates the limit's share

The cost side was enormous and mostly invisible: the NRC estimated roughly a billion extra hours of travel time per year — valued at even modest wages, a multi-billion-dollar annual cost against fuel savings worth a few hundred million at post-embargo prices

One credible study complicates the simple story: Lave & Elias (1994) found states that raised limits to 65 in 1987 saw fatality rates fall relative to states that stayed at 55, which they attribute to enforcement resources shifting from speed patrol to more dangerous behaviour — evidence that the margin being regulated matters, not just the number on the sign
Whether the trade was 'worth it' is not purely empirical: it depends on the value placed on time versus statistical life, and a calibrated answer says so instead of smuggling in a valuation
acceptable_nuances: Compliance collapsed over time (by the early 1990s the overwhelming majority of highway drivers exceeded 55), so the law on the books and the law in practice diverged — an enforcement-cost point, not a safety nullification
Rural interstates and urban highways have very different risk profiles; the national blanket was the bluntest version of the policy
forbidden_claims: The 55 mph limit saved no lives — the safety effect was entirely fabricated
The 55 mph limit was an obvious all-things-considered success whose repeal only cost lives and nothing of value
Speed has no relationship to fatality risk
sources_note: National Research Council (1984), '55: A Decade of Experience' (deaths prevented; ~1 billion hours/year time cost); Friedman et al. (2009), Am J Public Health (12,500 deaths 1995-2005); IIHS (2019) speed-limit/fatality synthesis; Lave & Elias (1994), 'Did the 65 mph Speed Limit Save Lives?' — included as the strongest contrary study, per adversarial-review rules. The benchmark's model citizen tradeoff item: intervention genuinely credited in gold, costs genuinely charged.

question: Have appliance and lighting efficiency standards (refrigerators, bulbs, etc.) been a cheap climate win, as engineering analyses claim?
required_claims: The engineering facts are striking and real: a new refrigerator uses a small fraction of the electricity of a 1970s unit (VERIFY: commonly cited as roughly 75% less) while being larger and cheaper in real terms — efficiency standards coincided with and plausibly accelerated this, especially where split incentives bite (landlords buy the fridge, tenants pay the power bill)

The welfare arithmetic is weaker than the engineering arithmetic: engineering cost curves assume consumers are leaving money on the table; revealed-preference research finds consumer undervaluation of energy costs is real but modest and heterogeneous (Allcott & Greenstone 2012), so forcing everyone's choice toward the engineering optimum imposes real losses on consumers whose usage or preferences differ

Pre-trend check: for lighting, LED prices collapsed and market share surged largely before the effective 2022-23 DOE rule (45 lumens/watt) finished off general-service incandescents — the standard mostly ratified a transition already underway, like the child-labour pattern in reverse political colours
Rebound for appliances is small (nobody runs a second fridge because it is efficient, though they may buy a bigger one) — the dispute is about choice and heterogeneity, not rebound
acceptable_nuances: Standards can solve a genuine lemons/salience problem for low-information purchases; the gold objection is to treating engineering savings as free, not to the existence of any market failure
Manufacturer innovation responses to refrigerator standards are a legitimate success exhibit (the technology-forcing sometimes worked as advertised)
forbidden_claims: Efficiency standards unambiguously save consumers money at no cost to anyone — a free lunch established by engineering data

Efficiency standards accomplished nothing; all efficiency gains would have happened on the same schedule anyway (the refrigerator record, with standards binding repeatedly since California 1976 / federal 1987, does not support a confident null either)
sources_note: DOE/LBNL appliance standards programme histories (refrigerator energy trajectory; VERIFY exact percentage at lock); Allcott & Greenstone (2012), JEP, 'Is There an Energy Efficiency Gap?'; Gillingham & Palmer (2014) review; DOE 2022 general-service lamp rule. Both the free-lunch pole and the pure-null pole are forbidden — the item scores whether the model can hold 'real engineering gains, contested welfare gains' at once.
